objectives: Nhận diện câu hỏi dạng WHY trong vòng 2 giây

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 7.5+
bookModels.question: Why do people enjoy spending time in natural places?
lines: People are drawn to natural environments for several interconnected reasons.

Psychologically speaking, nature has a well-documented calming effect on the human mind. Research consistently shows that spending time outdoors reduces cortisol levels — the hormone most associated with stress. In our increasingly screen-dominated lives, green spaces offer a rare opportunity to simply switch off. From a practical standpoint, natural settings provide an ideal backdrop for physical activity — hiking, cycling, swimming — which in turn improves overall fitness and sleep quality.

On a social level, visiting parks or the countryside is often a shared experience. Families bond over weekend walks, friends reconnect on camping trips, and communities come together at outdoor festivals. It satisfies a deeply human need for connection — both with other people and with the natural world.
For all these reasons, I think access to natural spaces is genuinely important for well-being, not just a luxury.

Phân tích cho học sinh: đếm số lần xuất hiện từ "because" trong bài mẫu — KHÔNG CÓ LẦN NÀO. Mỗi lý do đều được đánh dấu bằng một cụm chuyển tầng, và mỗi lý do đều có ít nhất một câu triển khai. Câu cuối có sắc thái ("not just a luxury") chứ không tóm tắt lại.

I think people like nature because it is relaxing. When you go to the park or the mountain, you feel comfortable and you can forget about your work. Also it is good for health because you walk a lot. And it is free, you do not need to pay money. So many people like it.
→Có ba ý nhưng đều nằm ở tầng thực tế/cảm giác chung. Dùng "because" ba lần. Không có cụm chuyển tầng nào. Khoảng 30 giây.
**BAND 7**

People are drawn to natural places for several reasons. Psychologically speaking, being outdoors helps reduce stress — after a long week in front of a screen, a walk in the park is a real escape. From a practical standpoint, nature encourages people to be physically active, which improves both fitness and sleep. And on a social level, it is usually something people do together, so it strengthens relationships as well. For all these reasons, I think access to green space matters a lot.
→Đủ ba tầng, có cụm chuyển tầng, có câu kết. Đây là mục tiêu tối thiểu của Lesson 1. Khoảng 55 giây.
**BAND 8**

People are drawn to natural environments for several interconnected reasons. Psychologically, nature has a well-documented calming effect — research consistently links time outdoors with lower cortisol levels, and in our increasingly screen-dominated lives that kind of switching off has become genuinely rare. From a practical standpoint, natural settings are simply the most accessible setting for exercise, which feeds back into sleep quality and general health. On a social level, it satisfies a deeply human need for connection: families bond over weekend walks, communities gather at outdoor festivals. For all these reasons, I would argue access to nature is a matter of public health rather than a lifestyle preference.

→Thêm bằng chứng cụ thể ("cortisol levels"), thêm liên kết giữa các lý do ("which feeds back into"), và câu kết định khung lại vấn đề ("public health rather than a lifestyle preference") thay vì tóm tắt.

lessons.title: Buổi 2 — DẠNG 2: OPINION
objectives: Không bao giờ trả lời Yes/No đơn lẻ cho câu hỏi Opinion

Kết bằng một câu có điều kiện, không phải một câu tóm tắt

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 7.5+
bookModels.question: Do you think it's important for children to learn a musical instrument?
lines: To a certain extent, yes — I think learning music offers real benefits for children. But I'd stop short of saying it should be compulsory for everyone.

On one hand, the cognitive benefits are well-established. Learning an instrument requires reading notation, developing hand-eye coordination, and maintaining focus for extended periods — all of which strengthen the brain in ways that transfer to academic performance. Children who study music often show stronger memory and concentration skills.

On the other hand, forcing every child to learn an instrument could easily backfire. Children have vastly different interests and abilities, and a one-size-fits-all approach risks creating resentment towards music rather than an appreciation for it. The key, I think, is exposure — giving children the opportunity to try various instruments and then letting them pursue what genuinely excites them.
On balance, music education is valuable, but its benefits only really materialise when children engage with it willingly rather than under compulsion.

Phân tích: câu đầu ĐÃ trả lời câu hỏi (yes) nhưng có giới hạn ngay. Câu cuối vẫn chọn bên (valuable) nhưng gắn điều kiện (willingly rather than under compulsion). Đây chính là "cân bằng nhưng vẫn có quan điểm".

lines: **BAND 6**
Yes, I think it is important. Music is good for children because it makes them happy and relaxed. Also they can play in a band with friends. So I think all children should learn a musical instrument.
→Trả lời một chiều, không có mặt giới hạn nào. Kết luận cực đoan ("all children"). Khoảng 25 giây.
**BAND 7**

To a certain extent, yes. On one hand, learning an instrument develops concentration and discipline, and there is quite a lot of research showing it helps with memory and even maths. On the other hand, I would stop short of saying every child must do it — children have very different interests, and forcing them can make them dislike music completely. On balance, I think schools should offer it, but let children choose.
→Đủ bốn bước, có sắc thái, kết luận có điều kiện. Đây là mục tiêu tối thiểu của Lesson 2. Khoảng 50 giây.
**BAND 8**

To a certain extent, yes — the benefits are real, but I would stop short of calling it essential. On one hand, the cognitive case is well established: reading notation, coordinating both hands and sustaining attention for long stretches all appear to transfer to academic performance. On the other hand, compulsion tends to backfire. A one-size-fits-all music policy risks producing resentment rather than appreciation, which is precisely the opposite of what it sets out to do. The key, I think, is exposure — letting children try several instruments and then pursue whichever one actually holds their attention. On balance, music education is valuable, but its benefits only really materialise when children engage with it willingly.
→Thêm chi tiết kỹ thuật cụ thể, thêm một câu nêu nghịch lý ("precisely the opposite of what it sets out to do"), và kết bằng một điều kiện có sức nặng thay vì một lời khuyên chung chung.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 7.5+
bookModels.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of working from home?
lines: Remote working is very much a double-edged sword — the benefits are real, but so are the costs, and they tend to fall on different groups of people.

The main benefit is autonomy. Employees can structure their day around when they actually work best, rather than around a fixed office schedule, and the time saved on commuting is substantial — for someone in a large city that can easily be two hours a day. There is also a financial dimension: lower transport costs for staff, and lower office costs for employers.

That said, the convenience comes at a cost. A significant drawback is the erosion of informal communication. A great deal of learning at work happens through overhearing colleagues and asking quick questions across a desk, and that simply does not translate to scheduled video calls. Junior staff are hit hardest — they lose the mentoring that used to happen almost by accident.

On balance, I think the benefits outweigh the drawbacks, provided that companies deliberately design in the contact that used to happen naturally. The trade-off is essentially between individual flexibility and collective cohesion, and it has to be managed rather than left to chance.

Phân tích: bất lợi ở đây có NGƯỜI CHỊU THIỆT cụ thể (junior staff) và CƠ CHẾ cụ thể (mất mentoring tình cờ). Câu kết không đếm số lượng mà nêu một điều kiện ("provided that…") và định nghĩa lại sự đánh đổi.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 7.5+
bookModels.question: How has the way people shop changed compared to the past?
lines: Shopping has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past two decades, driven almost entirely by digital technology.

In the past, shopping was an inherently physical and social activity. People visited local markets, browsed department stores at leisure, and relied on the advice of shop assistants. The entire process was slower, more deliberate, and embedded in community life.

Today, by contrast, convenience is the overriding priority. Online platforms allow consumers to compare prices, read thousands of reviews, and receive goods within hours — all without leaving their homes. The rise of social media has also created an entirely new form of shopping impulse, where a single post from an influencer can generate thousands of sales overnight.

That said, the two approaches are not entirely opposed. Many consumers now practise what is called webrooming — researching online but purchasing in-store — which suggests people value both the efficiency of digital shopping and the tangible experience of physical retail.
Ultimately, I think the most significant shift is in the power dynamic: consumers today are far better informed and have far more choices than any previous generation.

Phân tích: hai khía cạnh rõ ràng — tính xã hội (đoạn 2 và 3) và quyền lực thông tin (đoạn cuối). Đoạn 4 là điểm chung, chống lại lối so sánh một chiều. Câu cuối KHÔNG tóm tắt mà chọn ra một khác biệt quan trọng nhất.

4. Khoảng 70 giây.

In the past it was an inherently physical and social activity — people browsed at leisure, relied on shop assistants, and the whole process was slower, more deliberate and embedded in community life. bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER 1 — BAND 8 (DẠNG CHÍNH PHỦ)
bookModels.question: Do you think the government should do more to protect the environment?
lines: I think governments do have a critical responsibility here — but the nature of that responsibility matters enormously.

There are things only governments can realistically do: setting binding emissions targets, enforcing environmental regulations on corporations, and investing in large-scale renewable infrastructure. These require the kind of legal authority and financial resources that no individual or company can match. In that sense, stronger government action is not just desirable — it is necessary.

That said, I would be cautious about governments overreaching. Heavy-handed policies that restrict personal choices without providing viable alternatives tend to generate public backlash and are ultimately counterproductive. The most effective environmental policies I am aware of — carbon pricing schemes in Scandinavia, for example — succeed because they create economic incentives rather than simply imposing penalties.

Ultimately, I believe the most durable solutions emerge when governments lead by creating the right framework, businesses innovate within it, and individuals are educated and empowered to make better choices. It is a three-way responsibility, not one that falls entirely on any single party.
Phân tích: đoạn 2 nói rõ chỉ chính phủ mới làm được gì (authority + resources). Đoạn 3 nêu giới hạn kèm LÝ DO (backlash) và một ví dụ có thật. Câu cuối là mẫu câu kết vàng của dạng này.

bookModels.title: UPGRADE: BAND 6 → 7 → 8
bookModels.question: Do you think the government should do more to protect the environment?
lines: **BAND 6**

Yes, I think the government should do more. They should ban plastic bags and ban old cars because they pollute a lot. Also they should punish the factories that make pollution. And people should be more aware about the environment. If everybody does this, the environment will be better.
→Toàn bộ giải pháp là cấm và phạt. Giải pháp cuối không có chủ thể. Không có giới hạn nào. Khoảng 30 giây.
**BAND 7**

I think the government has an important role to play, but it should not be the only actor responsible. On one hand, only governments have the authority to set emissions targets and the money to invest in things like renewable energy or public transport — no individual can do that. However, I would be cautious about policies that simply restrict what people can do without giving them viable alternatives, because that usually generates public backlash. A more effective approach might be to incentivise rather than penalise: tax breaks for clean energy, for example. Ultimately I think it is a three-way responsibility between government, business and individuals.
→Đủ năm bước của khung 5B, có giới hạn kèm lý do, có câu kết trách nhiệm ba bên. Đây là mục tiêu tối thiểu của Lesson 5. Khoảng 70 giây.
**BAND 8**

Governments do have a critical responsibility here, but the nature of that responsibility matters enormously. There are things only governments can realistically do — setting binding emissions targets, enforcing regulations on large corporations, funding renewable infrastructure at national scale. These require legal authority and financial resources no individual or company can match, so in that sense stronger action is not merely desirable, it is necessary. That said, I would be cautious about overreach. Heavy-handed policies that restrict personal choice without providing viable alternatives tend to generate backlash and end up counterproductive. The environmental policies that have actually worked — carbon pricing in Scandinavia, for instance — succeed precisely because they create economic incentives rather than imposing penalties. Ultimately the most durable solutions emerge when governments create the right framework, businesses innovate within it, and individuals are equipped to make better choices. It is a three-way responsibility, not one that falls entirely on any single party.
→Có ví dụ chính sách có thật, có cụm phân biệt sắc thái ("not merely desirable, it is necessary"), và giải thích CƠ CHẾ vì sao chính sách kia thành công thay vì chỉ nêu tên.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER 1 — BAND 8 (DỰ ĐOÁN)
bookModels.question: How do you think cities will change in the future?
lines: Looking at current trends, I think cities are on the cusp of some genuinely transformative changes — though the pace will vary enormously depending on geography and economic development.

The most significant shift, I suspect, will be driven by climate pressures. Many cities are already retrofitting their infrastructure to cope with rising temperatures and extreme weather. We are likely to see a dramatic expansion of green spaces, vertical gardens and permeable surfaces designed to manage urban heat and water runoff — what planners call sponge cities.

Technology will reshape the physical fabric of cities too. Autonomous vehicles could render much of the existing road infrastructure redundant, freeing up the vast tracts of land currently devoted to parking. That land could be repurposed for housing or community facilities, which would be transformative in densely packed cities.

That said, predicting the future of cities is notoriously difficult. History is full of confident urban predictions that never materialised — flying cars, fully underground cities. The real drivers of change are often social and political rather than technological.
On balance, I would say the cities of 2050 will look recognisably similar to today, but with a much stronger emphasis on sustainability and human-scale design.
Phân tích: hai dự đoán, mỗi dự đoán có lực đẩy riêng (khí hậu, công nghệ). Đoạn 4 là caveat có bằng chứng lịch sử, không phải câu "but I am not sure" rỗng. Câu kết dự đoán mềm, có sắc thái.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER 2 — BAND 8 (THẾ HỆ)
bookModels.question: Do younger and older generations have different attitudes towards work?
lines: Yes, I think there is a fairly significant generational divide, though it is worth being careful not to overgeneralise.

Younger workers tend to prioritise purpose and flexibility over stability and salary. They are more likely to ask whether a job aligns with their values, or whether they can work remotely, than their parents would have. This is largely a product of growing up during economic instability and the rise of the gig economy — a context that made traditional employment feel less guaranteed anyway.

Older generations, shaped by different economic realities, often view work through a lens of loyalty and long- term commitment. Job security and seniority matter more to them — values instilled during a period when a career with a single employer was both achievable and aspirational.

Having said that, the distinction is not absolute. I know plenty of young people who crave stability, and older workers who have embraced remote work enthusiastically. Technology and shifting social norms have blurred generational lines considerably.
On balance, I would say the difference is less about work ethic — both generations work hard — and more about what they expect work to give them beyond a pay cheque.
Phân tích: mỗi thế hệ đều được giải thích bằng BỐI CẢNH KINH TẾ đã hình thành nên họ, không phải bằng phán xét. Đoạn 4 chống tuyệt đối hoá. Câu kết định nghĩa lại khác biệt ở một tầng sâu hơn.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER 1 — BAND 7.5+ (DẠNG PROBLEM/SOLUTION)
bookModels.question: How can education help children develop their own ideas?
lines: Education plays a foundational role in developing independent thought, though the extent to which it succeeds depends heavily on how it is delivered.

The most effective approaches tend to be those that prioritise questioning over memorisation. When teachers encourage students to challenge assumptions, debate different perspectives and arrive at their own conclusions — rather than simply reproducing correct answers — they are cultivating genuine intellectual independence. Project-based learning and Socratic discussion methods are particularly powerful in this regard. However, it is worth acknowledging that many education systems are still heavily oriented towards standardised testing, which inevitably rewards conformity over creativity. Students who think differently from the expected answer are often penalised rather than celebrated.
On balance, I think education has enormous potential to develop original thinkers — but only when it prioritises the process of thinking over the content of the answer.

Phân tích: giải pháp có CHỦ THỂ (teachers) và có PHƯƠNG PHÁP cụ thể (project-based learning, Socratic discussion). Đoạn 3 là giới hạn có cơ chế rõ (standardised testing rewards conformity). Câu kết là điều kiện, không phải lời khuyên chung.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER 2 — BAND 7.5+ (DẠNG OPINION)
bookModels.question: Do children usually share the same opinions as their parents?
lines: To a large degree, yes — but this influence tends to diminish as children mature and gain more exposure to the wider world.

Research in developmental psychology consistently shows that parents are the primary shapers of a child early values and worldview. This is simply a function of proximity and dependency — children learn by observing and imitating the adults closest to them.

However, as children enter adolescence and encounter peers, teachers, social media and broader cultural influences, their opinions begin to diverge, often quite significantly. This is a normal and, I would argue, healthy developmental process. A society in which every generation simply mirrored the values of the one before it would be a society incapable of progress.

Having said that, the degree of divergence varies enormously depending on cultural context. In more collectivist societies, intergenerational value transmission tends to be stronger and more deliberately maintained.

Phân tích: câu mở có sắc thái ("to a large degree… but"). Đoạn 3 có một câu lập luận trừu tượng mạnh ("a society incapable of progress") — đây là chi tiết đẩy bài từ Band 7 lên 7.5+. Đoạn cuối thêm chiều văn hoá.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 8
bookModels.question: Does technology make people lazier?
lines: This is a question I find genuinely interesting, because the reality is more nuanced than a simple yes or no. In some respects, technology has clearly reduced the physical and cognitive effort required for everyday tasks. Navigation apps mean we no longer memorise routes; autocorrect compensates for poor spelling; streaming services mean we never have to tolerate boredom. There is a reasonable argument that this systematic reduction in friction is gradually eroding our tolerance for difficulty.

However, I would push back on the idea that this is straightforwardly laziness. Technology has freed up cognitive bandwidth that was previously consumed by routine tasks, allowing people to direct their energy towards more complex and creative work. The question is whether people actually use that freed-up time productively — and that is more a function of personal discipline and social environment than of technology itself.

On balance, I think technology amplifies existing tendencies rather than creating new ones. A motivated person uses it to achieve more; a less motivated person uses it to avoid effort. The tool is neutral — the user is not.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 8
bookModels.question: Do you think individuals can make a real difference to the environment?
lines: I think individuals can make a meaningful difference, but it is important to be honest about the limits of individual action in isolation.

The most optimistic argument for individual agency is that collective behaviour drives market forces. When enough consumers refuse single-use plastics, producers adapt. When enough people choose plant-based diets, the food industry responds. History gives us examples — the dramatic decline in CFC use following public awareness campaigns about the ozone layer — where behavioural shifts have contributed to measurable environmental improvements.

However, research consistently shows that a disproportionate share of global carbon emissions comes from a small number of large industrial actors. There is a genuine risk that the emphasis on individual responsibility functions as a deflection, allowing corporations and governments to avoid accountability by placing the burden on consumers.

On balance, I would say individual action is necessary but not sufficient. It works best as part of a broader ecosystem of change that includes stringent regulation, corporate accountability and systemic investment in sustainable infrastructure.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 8
bookModels.question: How important is it for people to help their local community?
lines: I think community engagement is more important now than at perhaps any point in recent history — precisely because the forces pulling communities apart have never been stronger.

Urbanisation, digital connectivity and increasingly mobile lifestyles have dramatically weakened the social fabric that used to hold communities together. People are less likely to know their neighbours, shop locally or participate in community institutions than previous generations were. The consequences are very real: higher rates of loneliness, reduced social trust, and a diminished capacity to address local problems collectively. Community involvement — whether through volunteering, local politics, or simply checking in on vulnerable neighbours — functions as a kind of social infrastructure. It creates the dense networks of mutual obligation that make communities resilient when crises occur.

That said, I think we need to be careful about placing excessive moral weight on community service. People capacity to engage is heavily shaped by economic circumstances — someone working two jobs and raising children alone simply has less time and energy than someone with more resources.
On balance, community engagement is genuinely valuable, but fostering it requires creating the social and economic conditions in which it is actually possible.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 8
bookModels.question: Why do some people find it difficult to maintain a healthy lifestyle?
lines: This is a question where it is tempting to give a simple answer — lack of willpower — but the reality is considerably more structural.

Time pressure is perhaps the most significant barrier. In societies where long working hours are normalised and commuting consumes hours each day, finding time to prepare nutritious meals and exercise regularly becomes genuinely difficult, not merely a matter of poor priorities.

Cost is another substantial factor. Fresh food tends to be considerably more expensive per calorie than processed alternatives, particularly in urban areas. The notion that healthy eating is simply a choice ignores the reality that for lower-income households, calorie density per unit of cost often has to take precedence. There is also a powerful environmental dimension. People make health decisions within contexts — if a neighbourhood lacks safe places to exercise, if a workplace canteen offers only fried food, if advertising constantly promotes high-sugar products, then choosing health means swimming against a very strong current. I think this is why purely education-based public health campaigns tend to have limited effect. Telling people what they should do, without changing the environment in which they make those decisions, rarely produces lasting change.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 8
bookModels.question: Why are some people very ambitious at work?
lines: Workplace ambition is driven by a fascinating mix of psychological, economic and social factors, and it is rarely reducible to a single cause.

At the individual level, ambition often stems from a deep-seated need for achievement, recognition or autonomy. For some people, career success is the primary arena in which they measure their self-worth — and that can be a product of upbringing, since children raised in highly achievement-oriented families often internalise the belief that success is both possible and mandatory.

Economics plays a significant role too. In societies with high income inequality, the gap between professional success and mediocrity can be enormous — not just in lifestyle, but in security, healthcare, housing and opportunities for one's children. Under those conditions, ambition is less about desire and more about necessity.

There is also a social dimension. In industries where ambition is culturally celebrated — investment banking, elite consulting, tech startups — the peer environment creates strong normative pressure to compete. Ambition becomes contagious.

Of course, not all ambition is healthy. When it becomes compulsive and crowds out other values — relationships, health, integrity — it can be deeply counterproductive. The most admirable ambition, in my view, is directed towards creating genuine value rather than accumulating status.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 8
bookModels.question: What advantages can tourism bring to a city?
lines: Tourism can bring substantial benefits to cities, though those benefits are distributed unevenly and come with real costs.

The most direct advantage is economic. Visitor spending generates revenue for hotels, restaurants, transport and retail, creating jobs across a wide spectrum of skill levels. In cities with significant historical assets, tourism can become a major economic pillar — think of how central it is to Venice, Kyoto or Prague.

Beyond economics, tourism plays a meaningful role in cultural preservation. Revenue generated by visitor interest often funds the conservation work that local governments could not otherwise afford. In that sense, tourism and heritage can form a virtuous cycle.
There are softer benefits too — the presence of international visitors exposes residents to different perspectives and ways of life, which enriches the cultural texture of a city over time.

That said, it would be dishonest to ignore the downsides. Over-tourism prices local residents out of their own neighbourhoods, strains infrastructure, and erodes the very authenticity that made a place attractive in the first place. The challenge for planners is harnessing the economic benefits while managing the social and environmental costs — a balance very few cities have achieved.

Phân tích: câu mở đã báo trước tính phân bổ không đồng đều. Ba lợi ích thuộc ba loại khác nhau (kinh tế, văn hoá, xã hội). Đoạn cuối nêu nghịch lý và kết bằng một nhận định thực tế, không lạc quan giả.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER — BAND 8
bookModels.question: How has social media changed the way people communicate?
lines: Social media has fundamentally restructured human communication in ways that are simultaneously empowering and deeply problematic.

On the empowering side, it has dramatically lowered the barriers to connection and self-expression. People maintain relationships across continents with minimal effort, organise social and political movements in real time, and find communities of shared interest that could not have existed before. For marginalised voices in particular — people historically excluded from mainstream media — platforms have created genuine opportunities for visibility.

However, the structural incentives of these platforms — designed to maximise engagement rather than well- being — have introduced some alarming dynamics. An algorithmically curated feed rewards outrage, simplification and tribal signalling over nuance. Echo chambers form and harden. Misinformation spreads faster than corrections. Public discourse has become simultaneously more accessible and less thoughtful. I think the most significant long-term shift is the collapse of the distinction between private and public communication. Things once said only to close friends are now broadcast to thousands, often with consequences neither party anticipated.
On balance, social media is a genuinely powerful tool that we have not yet developed the cultural norms or regulatory frameworks to use wisely.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER 1 — BAND 8 (FAMILY)
bookModels.question: How have family structures changed in recent decades?
lines: Family structures have undergone a profound transformation over the past fifty years, reflecting broader shifts in economic organisation, gender roles and cultural values.

The most significant change has been the decline of the traditional nuclear family — a married couple with a male breadwinner and female homemaker — as the dominant model. Several factors drove this. The large- scale entry of women into the workforce fundamentally altered household economics. Rising divorce rates normalised single-parent families. Greater legal acceptance of same-sex partnerships expanded the definition of family itself.

At the same time, urbanisation has weakened extended family networks. Previous generations could rely on grandparents, aunts and cousins living within walking distance. In a mobile professional society that proximity is rare, which has increased individual autonomy but, for many people, intensified isolation.

It is worth noting that these changes are not uniform. In more collectivist cultures — across much of Asia, the Middle East and sub-Saharan Africa — extended family structures remain not merely culturally valued but economically essential.

I think the key challenge for modern societies is building support systems — affordable childcare, elderly care, mental health services — that compensate for the reduced capacity of the family to meet all its members needs.

bookModels.title: MODEL ANSWER 2 — BAND 8 (ARTS)
bookModels.question: Should governments fund the arts?
lines: I think there is a strong case for government arts funding, though the debate is more nuanced than advocates on either side usually acknowledge.

The core argument rests on the idea that the arts generate social value the market consistently underprices. Literature, music, theatre and visual art contribute to cultural cohesion and the quality of civic life in ways that cannot easily be monetised. If funding were left entirely to market forces, we would end up with a cultural landscape dominated by whatever is commercially profitable — which is not the same thing as what is culturally valuable.

There is also an equity argument. Without public funding, participation in the arts, both as creator and as audience, becomes increasingly the preserve of the wealthy. Publicly funded theatres, galleries and orchestras make culture accessible to people who could never afford commercial prices.

That said, critics are right to raise questions about allocation. Too often, funding disproportionately benefits established institutions serving already privileged audiences. A genuinely democratic arts policy would prioritise grassroots and community-based work alongside elite institutions.
On balance, governments have a legitimate role in supporting the arts — but that role requires constant scrutiny to ensure it serves the broadest possible public.
Phân tích: hai lập luận ủng hộ thuộc hai loại khác nhau (giá trị và công bằng), một lập luận phản biện có tính xây dựng, và câu kết đặt điều kiện giám sát — không phải một lời ủng hộ vô điều kiện.
